<reason>The debate crystallized into one question: what counts as "tradition" — the ancient core (vows, witnesses, family, meal) or whatever is enforced under tradition's name. B won that clash decisively. B offered a principled test (old, cross-cultural, enacting rather than displaying), tied it to the motion's own inferential structure (expense as parasite, not host, making the motion a non sequitur as written), and exposed A's rival criterion as circular, inconsistent with A1.5's own diamond/marketing distinction, and self-defeating (it would dissolve obligation to A's own curated alternatives once enforced). B also converted A's concessions (promises need witnesses; twenty chosen people suffice) into B's case, and answered both pressure questions cleanly (duty to a person ≠ duty to every demand in her name). A was rhetorically superb and its concession-capture of B ("one family's guess") was clever, but that move depended entirely on the sociological definition B dismantled, and A's list of skippable "traditional" items turned out to be either commercial or the family presence B defended. Both sides were disciplined (no fake sourcing, clean format, proper Q/A structure), but B made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Q2 (what criterion separates the enforced diamond called "marketing" from the enforced guest list called "tradition") forced A4.2's circular answer — tradition is whatever is enforced under its name — which B4.4 dismantled three ways: circularity, contradiction with A1.5, and proving too much. "If enforcement defines tradition, the marketing department writes the dictionary" sealed the definitional clash that decided the motion.</best_rebuttal>
